title: Verification asks one question: does the error fall at the order the scheme promises?
summary: A solver is verified when its error shrinks at the theoretical rate as the grid is refined. The observed order, Richardson extrapolation, the grid convergence index and a manufactured solution are four tools for answering that, and none of them says whether the equations are the right ones.

media.alt: Log-log plot of error against grid spacing h from 0.001 to 0.3 for three synthetic schemes of order 1, 2 and 4. Each is a straight line, steeper for higher order, and a dotted horizontal line near 1e-14 marks the round-off floor.
media.caption: Reference render of plot class F5.1 with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery), not a project result.

source.note: Standard numerical analysis and the verification literature (Roache). The figure is the design system's synthetic F5.1 render, so no project number is quoted.

read_the_figure.question: What is the observed order of accuracy, and does it match the order the scheme was designed to have?
read_the_figure.axes: x: grid spacing h on a log scale (fine on the left, coarse on the right). y: error against a known reference on a log scale. Each marker is one complete solve on one grid.
look_at: The slope of each line on these axes is the order $p$: error $\approx C h^p$ becomes $\log E = \log C + p\log h$, a straight line of slope $p$.
Order 4 falls by about four decades for each decade of $h$; order 1 loses only one. Compare the slope with the order in the legend, not the height of the line.
The dotted floor is round-off: below it, refining the grid cannot help because the arithmetic, not the scheme, sets the error.
Only the straight part counts. At coarse $h$ the error has not yet entered its asymptotic range.
read_the_figure.proves: Lines that stay parallel to their design slope over several grid levels show that the code solves the discretised equations at the rate claimed. That is verification.
if_wrong: A shallower slope than designed: something does not refine with $h$ (a time step held fixed, a first-order boundary condition, a source term evaluated at low order, or a bug).
A curve that flattens at the fine end: round-off, an iteration tolerance that is too loose, or a floor from a fixed time step.
A slope that changes from one pair of grids to the next: the grids are not in the asymptotic range, so no single order should be quoted.
must_check: Both axes logarithmic, with the same decades per unit length so the slope is not distorted.
A reference line of the designed slope drawn beside the data.
The error norm named (L1, L2 or max) and the reference stated (exact, manufactured or finest-grid).
Time step refined together with the grid, or stated to be fixed.

terms.meaning: What is left over when the exact solution is substituted into the discrete equations: the Taylor terms the scheme throws away.
The exponent $p$ in error $\approx C h^p$. Halving $h$ divides the error by $2^p$.
Coarse spacing divided by fine spacing between two grids. Use a constant ratio, 2 is common.
The exponent measured from solutions on several grids. It need not equal the formal order, and the difference is the diagnostic.
Combining two grid solutions to cancel the leading error term and estimate the grid-independent value.
Roache's standard way to report discretisation uncertainty: the extrapolation difference times a safety factor, as a percentage.
A smooth function chosen first; the source term that makes it an exact solution is computed afterwards, so the exact answer is known.
How many cells a wave crosses in one time step. It controls stability of explicit schemes.
The factor by which one Fourier mode is multiplied each step. Stable means its magnitude never exceeds 1.
Verification: are we solving the equations right? Validation: are they the right equations? Different evidence answers each.

remember: Error $\approx C h^p$, so the slope of $\log E$ against $\log h$ is $p$.
Two grids: $p=\ln(E_2/E_1)/\ln r$. Three grids with ratio $r$: $p=\ln\!\big[(f_3-f_2)/(f_2-f_1)\big]/\ln r$, with 1 the finest grid.
GCI (fine grid) $=F_s\,|\varepsilon|/(r^p-1)$ with $\varepsilon=(f_2-f_1)/f_1$, $F_s=1.25$ for three grids and 3 for two.
FTCS for the heat equation is stable only for $r=\alpha\Delta t/\Delta x^2\le\tfrac12$. FTCS for advection is unstable for every $c$. First-order upwind needs $0\le c\le1$.
A converged code can still solve the wrong model: verification does not replace validation.

understand.title: Intuition
understand.text: A scheme of order $p$ is a promise about a rate, not about a size: halve the spacing and the error drops by $2^p$. The promise can only be tested by solving the same problem on several grids and watching the rate. If the rate matches, the code does what the algebra says. If it does not, either the algebra was not what you coded or something else (time step, boundary, tolerance) is limiting.

understand.title: What the three tools add
understand.text: The observed order tells you the rate. Richardson extrapolation uses that rate to estimate where the error is heading, giving a better number and a free error estimate. The GCI wraps that estimate in a conservative safety factor so that different studies can be reported in the same way. A manufactured solution supplies the exact answer when the real problem has none, so the first tool becomes available for any equation.

understand.title: The hard tier
understand.text: Everything above assumes the error is dominated by one power of $h$. That is only true in the asymptotic range, which for a nonlinear, shocked or turbulent flow may need grids you cannot afford. Mixed-order effects (a second-order scheme with a first-order limiter near a front) give an observed order between 1 and 2 that is correct and not a bug. Stability is a separate question again: a scheme can be consistent and still diverge, and the Lax equivalence theorem says that for linear problems consistency plus stability is exactly convergence.

steps.title: Truncation error of two difference formulas
steps.note: Verified with a symbolic Taylor series. The first formula is first order, the second is second order, and the leading coefficient depends on the solution's own derivatives.

steps.title: The error model and the observed order from two grids
steps.note: On a log-log plot this is the slope between two points. It needs the exact answer, which is why the next steps matter.

steps.title: Three grids: the order without knowing the exact answer
steps.note: Subtracting neighbouring grids removes the unknown $f_e$. Grid 1 is the finest. Verified symbolically for a constant ratio $r$.

steps.title: Richardson extrapolation
steps.note: Substituting the three-grid model shows this equals $f_e$ exactly when the model holds. In practice it is accurate to the next order in $h$, and it is only as good as the assumption that both grids lie in the asymptotic range.

steps.title: The grid convergence index
steps.note: Roache's recommendation is $F_s=1.25$ when three grids confirm the order, and $F_s=3$ when only two grids are used. It reports an uncertainty band, not an error: the band should contain the fine-grid error.

steps.title: Manufacture a solution
steps.tex: u_t+a\,u_x-\nu\,u_{xx}=s(x,t),\quad u_m=e^{-t}\sin\pi x\;\Rightarrow\; s=e^{-t}\big[(\nu\pi^2-1)\sin\pi x+a\pi\cos\pi x\big]
steps.note: Pick any smooth $u_m$, apply the operator, call the result the source, and add it to the code. The code must now reproduce $u_m$, so the error is known on every grid. Verified symbolically. Choose $u_m$ to exercise every term, and take boundary values from it.

steps.title: Von Neumann stability: one Fourier mode
steps.note: Insert a single mode into the linear scheme. The amplification factor $G$ is what one step does to that mode.

steps.title: FTCS heat equation: the diffusion number
steps.note: The worst mode is $\theta=\pi$, where $G=1-4r$. At $r=0.55$ that is $-1.2$, so the sawtooth grows by 20 percent per step. This is the failure the atlas shows.

steps.title: Advection: FTCS fails for every step, upwind needs the CFL condition
steps.note: Central differencing in space with a forward step in time amplifies every mode with $\sin\theta\neq0$, however small $c$. Upwinding is stable up to $c=1$: information must not cross more than one cell per step (Courant, Friedrichs and Lewy 1928). Both verified symbolically.

steps.title: Verification is not validation
steps.note: Roache's phrasing is that verification is solving the equations right and validation is solving the right equations. A perfect convergence plot says nothing about whether a turbulence model, a reaction mechanism or a boundary condition describes the real flow.

worked.title: Observed order, extrapolation and GCI from three grids
worked.problem: The central difference $(\sin(1+h)-\sin(1-h))/(2h)$ approximates $\cos 1$. Treat the exact value as unknown. Grids $h=0.4,\,0.2,\,0.1$ (so $r=2$) give $f_3=0.52601$, $f_2=0.53671$, $f_1=0.53940$. Find the observed order, the Richardson estimate and the fine-grid GCI.

solution.text: Observed order, ratio of the two differences.
Richardson extrapolation with the observed order.
Relative change between the two finest grids, then the GCI with $F_s=1.25$.

worked.answer: Observed order 1.99 (design order 2), extrapolated value 0.54031, GCI 0.21 percent. The actual fine-grid error is 0.17 percent, inside the band. Extrapolation cuts the error by about two orders of magnitude, from 9e-4 to 7e-6. Numbers computed and checked with a script.

analyze.q: A convergence study gives observed orders 1.98, 1.91 and 1.62 for three successive pairs of grids. Is the scheme second order? What would you do next?
analyze.hint: The order is drifting, so which pairs are in the asymptotic range?

analyze.q: Explain in terms of the amplification factor why FTCS applied to $u_t+au_x=0$ blows up even at a tiny CFL number, while FTCS for the heat equation is fine at $r=0.4$.
A manufactured solution that is a single low-degree polynomial passes the order test at every grid. Why is that a weak verification?
analyze.hint: A second-order stencil is exact for quadratics, so some error terms vanish.

evaluate.q: A report quotes 'GCI = 0.3 percent' computed from two grids with $F_s=1.25$. What is wrong with the claim?
evaluate.hint: Which factor goes with which number of grids?

evaluate.q: A solver reproduces its manufactured solution to the designed order. Does that show the simulation of a real flame, or a real jet, is correct?

create: Design a manufactured solution for the 2D incompressible momentum equations. Which properties must $u_m$ and $p_m$ have, and how do you handle the continuity equation?
Write the test that runs a solver on four grids, computes the pairwise observed orders and fails automatically if the finest pair is more than 0.2 from the design order.

checks.q: Why is the slope on a log-log error plot equal to the order of accuracy?
checks.hint: Take the logarithm of error = C h^p.
checks.answer: Because $E=Ch^p$ gives $\log E=\log C+p\log h$, a straight line in $\log h$ whose slope is $p$. Halving $h$ moves one step left and the error drops by $2^p$.

checks.q: Errors are 4.0e-3 at $h=0.1$ and 1.0e-3 at $h=0.05$. What is the observed order?
checks.answer: $p=\ln 4/\ln 2=2$. The scheme behaves as second order.

checks.q: FTCS for the heat equation runs at $r=0.55$ and the solution turns into a sawtooth that grows. Which mode is responsible and by how much does it grow per step?
checks.answer: The highest-frequency mode, $\theta=\pi$ (alternating sign on every cell). There $G=1-4r=-1.2$, so it flips sign and grows by a factor 1.2 every step. At $r=0.5$ it neither grows nor decays.

checks.q: A group shows a perfect second-order slope using the solution on the finest grid as 'exact'. What is weak about that?
checks.hint: Does that reference contain the same error source as the coarser grids?
checks.answer: The reference carries its own discretisation error and shares any modelling or implementation error with the coarser runs, so the slope shrinks towards the wrong target and a consistent bug can be hidden. A manufactured or analytic solution, or Richardson extrapolation with an explicit uncertainty, is a better reference.

checks.q: You have only a CFD code with a source-term input and no analytic solution. How do you verify it?
checks.answer: Pick a smooth $u_m$ that exercises every term, apply the continuous operator symbolically to get the source, add that source to the code, impose boundary values from $u_m$, solve on at least three grids with a constant ratio (refining the time step too), and check that the observed orders match the design orders.
